catalog_quote: Vowel contrast in Matngele relates to quality only; that is, there is no phonemic vowel length contrast. Yet long vowels do occur, optionally, in monosyllabic words, as in eg. ya: 'yes,' and lenitions, as in eg. mi: from miyi 'food' and wa:rri from wangarri 'you(sg)' (see section 2.6). Most long vowels occur in the first syllable of a morpheme, even if embedded within a complex word. For example, buy-a:ynju-wa 'you go and get' is typical for length distribution in Matngele. There are only three examples of a long vowel in the second syllable, again due to lenition, these are: amu:al 'Amungal', boda:n 'Darwin' (both place names), and with prosodic shift in interrogative buy-nung.ga:yn? 'are you going?'. new_statements.quote: Vowel contrast in Matngele relates to quality only; that is, there is no phonemic vowel length contrast. Yet long vowels do occur, optionally, in monosyllabic words ... Most long vowels occur in the first syllable of a morpheme, even if embedded within a complex word. ... Broadly, then, the distributional restrictions of Matngele long vowels concur with those described by Dixon (1980:132), in that they do not occur more than once per word; and generally coincide with the primary stress within the word, hence their preponderance in word initial syllables.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Indirect statement only: primary word stress is taken to fall on the word-initial syllable (non-phonemic long vowels line up with primary stress and therefore cluster in word-initial syllables; long vowels also favour the first syllable of a morpheme inside complex words). The thesis has no dedicated stress section and gives no explicit placement rule, secondary-stress rule, or stress-marked transcriptions.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for Matngele. (Sister language Kamu, Harvey 1989 sec. 2.12: secondary stress on every second syllable after a primary-stressed syllable, never adjacent to a primary stress or a word boundary; primary stress on the first syllable of each poly-moraic morpheme.)
new_statements.exceptions: Three words with a long vowel in the second syllable (amu:al 'Amungal', boda:n 'Darwin', and interrogative buy-nung.ga:yn? 'are you going?' 'with prosodic shift'), attributed to lenition/intonation rather than stated as stress exceptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('primary stress within the word'); remark also notes long vowels in the first syllable of a morpheme within complex (polysynthetic) words, hinting at morpheme-initial prominence as in Kamu. Data are second-hand (Laves 1931, Hoddinott 1967, Harvey field notes/tapes), not the author's own fieldwork.
new_statements.identity_note: Zandvoort 1999 describes Matngele proper (madn1237), synthesised from Laves 1931, Hoddinott 1967 and Harvey 1980s-90s field notes (speakers Edwin Purrel, Jack Marrurritj, Woolianna NT). The only full stress rule found is for the SISTER language Kamu (Harvey 1989, kamu1258 / ISO xmu), not for Matngele; it should not be entered under madn1237 but is a strong prior (both Eastern Daly). Tryon 1974 treats 'Matngala' with dialects Kamor and Yunggor.

sources.note: Ch. 2 Phonology (pp. 11-30: phonemes, allophones, phonotactics, lenition, stop contrast) has no stress section. Only statement, sec. 2.3.1.3 'Vowel length' p. 14: non-phonemic long vowels occur at most once per word 'and generally coincide with the primary stress within the word, hence their preponderance in word initial syllables' (i.e. primary stress implied word-initial). App. 3 p. [Laves text]: Laves' 1931 notes lack stress marking so word boundaries are unclear.

sources.citation: Harvey, Mark. 1989. A Sketch Grammar of Kamu. Unpublished manuscript, held at AIATSIS (retyped digital version, 116 pp., hosted at https://dalylanguages.org/files/Kamu%). [Sister language Kamu, kamu1258]
sources.note: KAMU, not Matngele. Sec. 2.12 'Stress' (pp. 26-27): every poly-moraic morpheme receives a primary stress 'placed on the first syllable'; monosyllabic major-class roots have long vowels and are stressed, other monosyllables unstressed; 'Secondary stresses are placed on every second syllable following a primary stressed syllable', never adjacent to a primary stress or a word boundary; main phonetic cue is pitch.
